lead: Chain and tape surveying fixes points by measuring straight distances with a chain or steel tape, then locates detail by a short offset from those lines. It needs no angle instrument — only a tape, ranging rods, arrows and a cross-staff — so it is cheap, quick and easy to check. The result is a skeleton of lines: a base line, tie lines and check lines. It suits house plots and small sites, and gives a first pass before a total station or EDM takes over.
prereq: You need: measurements, errors, accuracy and precision for error types and scales, maps and topographic sheets for how field distances become a map.

blocks.text: A chain is 100 or 150 links of galvanised steel wire, each link 0.2 m, with a brass handle at each end; a metric chain is 20 m or 30 m. A tape is a continuous strip — steel for routine work (10–50 m), invar where a base line must be precise because invar barely expands with heat, linen for rough work.

items: Ranging rods: 2 m or 3 m poles painted in 0.2 m red and white bands, so a station can be sighted far away.
Arrows (chain pins): 400 mm steel pins, ten to a set, dropped at every chain length.
Cross-staff: a staff with two sighting slits at right angles, for setting out a perpendicular from the chain line.
Optical square: two mirrors fixed at 45°, doing the same job with better accuracy.
Pegs and plumb bob: transfer a point from tape to ground.

blocks.text: Ranging is fixing intermediate points on the straight line between two stations. On level ground with both ends visible, one person stands behind a station and sights along the line, signalling the rodman to move left or right until the rod hides the far station. That is direct ranging. When the ends cannot see each other, two rodmen use indirect or reciprocal ranging: each can see one end station and lines in the other's rod towards it, and they repeat this in turns until both rods sit on the straight line between the two stations. On sloping ground the tape is held horizontal and stepped down in short lengths, or the slope length is measured and corrected (see below).

sections.h3: Base line, tie line, check line and offsets

blocks.text: Reconnaissance comes first: walk the site, note buildings, trees and the road, and sketch an index map showing the stations. Three kinds of line then build the framework.

items: Base line: longest line, through the middle on flattest ground, measured with greatest care because every other length is tied to it.
Tie line (subsidiary line): joins a survey station to a point on a main line, turning one long offset into two short ones.
Check line: joins two points already fixed. Its length can be computed from the triangles and also measured; the difference is the error of the whole job.

blocks.text: An offset is a short measurement from the chain line out to an object — fence corner, tree, manhole. Book two numbers: chainage (distance along the line from the start) and offset length. A perpendicular offset is at 90°, set with a cross-staff or optical square. An oblique offset is at any angle, used when a right angle is awkward. Keep offsets short. The longer the offset, the more a small error in setting the right angle moves the plotted point; the limiting length of an offset is the one at which that shift would just show on the plan, about 0.25 mm at the plotting scale.

items: Open field book so ruled page faces you; vertical line divides chainage from offset.
Enter chainage left of line and offset length right, same row.
Work up the page from bottom, chainage increasing.
Never erase: strike out a wrong entry and rewrite it, so the original survives.

blocks.text: Every tape has built-in error, and field conditions differ from the day it was standardized. Write correction c as the amount added to measured length M to get true length: true = M + c. Some books define c as measured − true, and then every sign flips; fix the convention first.

blocks.where: standardization: L′ true length between end marks (m), L nominal length (30 m), M measured length (m). Tape too long gives positive c.

temperature: α is the coefficient of expansion, about 11 to 12 × 10⁻⁶ per °C for steel (use the value the question gives), T field temperature (°C), T₀ standardization temperature (°C). Hotter than T₀ means tape expanded and reading is short, so c is positive.
tension: P applied pull (N), P₀ standard pull (N), A tape cross-section (mm²), E Young's modulus, 2.0 × 10⁵ N/mm² for steel. Harder pull stretches tape, reading short, c positive.
sag, for one span: w weight per metre (N/m), l unsupported span (m), P pull (N). For n equal spans multiply by n. A sagging tape bows below straight line and reads long, so c is negative.
slope and alignment: h level difference between ends (m), or distance tape is held off the line (m). Measured value is always longer, so c negative. Total correction is sum of all terms.

figure.caption: Top: the base line AC carries the survey; the check line BD tests the two triangles built on it, the tie line DE fixes detail far from the base, and short perpendicular offsets fix the house. Bottom: the 20.000 m slope length with a 1.200 m rise is 19.964 m in plan, a correction of −0.036 m.

examples.question: A 30 m steel tape was standardized at 20 °C. It is used at 35 °C to measure a line, and the reading is 30.000 m. The coefficient of thermal expansion of steel is 11.2 × 10⁻⁶ per °C. (a) Find the temperature correction and the true length. (b) A separate slope measurement between two stations is 20.000 m along the slope, with a level difference of 1.200 m between the ends. Find the horizontal distance and the slope correction.
steps: Temperature correction: c<sub>t</sub> = M α ΔT = 30.000 × 11.2 × 10⁻⁶ × 15 = 0.00504 m = +5.04 mm.
examples.answer: Temperature correction = +5.04 mm, giving a true length of 30.005 m; the horizontal distance is 19.964 m, a slope correction of −0.036 m.
examples.check:
L = 30.000
alpha = 11.2e-6
dT = 35 - 20
ct = L * alpha * dT
print(f"{ct:.5f}")
print(f"{L + ct:.5f}")
s = 20.000
h = 1.200
horiz = (s**2 - h**2) ** 0.5
print(f"{horiz:.3f}")
print(f"{horiz - s:.3f}")

traps: Sign convention: c = true − measured here. Books using measured − true flip every sign; state your convention before adding.

In the standardisation, temperature and tension formulas M is the measured length of the whole line, not the 30 m tape. In the sag formula l is one unsupported span: a 30 m tape supported every 10 m has three spans with l = 10 m, so the sag correction is 3 × w²(10)³/(24P²).
Units in tension formula: pull N, area mm², E N/mm². Mixing mm² with m² throws answer out by 10⁶.
Slope and alignment corrections are always negative; slope or off-line distance is longer than horizontal.
If check line disagrees, re-measure; never stretch offsets to close the figure.

quiz.q: Name the four main items of equipment used in chain and tape surveying, and state what each is for.
quiz.a: Chain or tape for lengths; ranging rods for sighting stations; arrows to mark each chain length; cross-staff or optical square for perpendicular offsets.

quiz.q: Why is the base line measured with more care than any other line?
quiz.a: Every other line and offset is tied to it, so its error enters the whole framework. It is also the longest line, so a small relative error is a large absolute error.

quiz.q: Distinguish a tie line from a check line.
quiz.a: A tie line joins a station to a point on a main line and is part of the framework. A check line joins two already fixed points and is measured only to test the framework.

quiz.q: A tape of nominal length 30 m is actually 0.008 m too short. It reads 180.000 m between two stations. Find the true distance.
A 30 m tape weighing 0.25 N/m is stretched at 100 N and supported only at its ends. Find the sag correction.
A check line measures 84.320 m while the framework gives 84.290 m. What does this tell you, and what should you do?
quiz.a: The framework is out by 84.320 − 84.290 = 0.030 m in about 84 m, a relative error of 0.030/84.29 = 1 in 2810. If the job asks for 1 in 5000, this fails. Re-measure the check line first, then the lines that fix its ends; never adjust offsets to force agreement.

quiz.q: What is the chainage of an offset?
quiz.a: The distance measured along the chain line from the start of the line to the point where the offset leaves it.

quiz.q: Why is a very long offset a risk, and how does a tie line help?
quiz.a: A long offset is hard to hold perpendicular, so a small angular error gives a large sideways error at the object; it also crosses other detail. A tie line brings the chain line closer, so the offset is short.

beyond: Not for the exam. Taping has not disappeared: an EDM or total station is still checked on a calibrated baseline, using the same standardization, temperature and sag terms. These corrections are also the standard worked example for systematic error in measurements, errors, accuracy and precision. Search next for invar baseline measurement, tape standardization and sag correction derivation, then compare with how EDM quotes accuracy as a constant plus parts per million.
